meta.title: Clustering and Dimensionality Reduction
meta.thesis: Clustering and Dimensionality Reduction is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A support team wants to discover ticket themes without labels and visualize them for ops review. By the end, they should be able to build or review clustering workflow with embeddings, projection, and cluster naming checks, measure cluster coherence judged by reviewers, and catch the failure where a pretty 2D plot creates fake confidence about weak clusters.

modules.title: Unlabeled data still needs a question
modules.sub: Clustering without a decision becomes decorative geometry.
modules.summary: Unsupervised learning should begin with a use case and validation plan.
objectives: Explain why cluster IDs are not ground truth.

blocks.title: Clusters are hypotheses about structure

spans.text: Problem anchor: a support team has 20,000 unlabeled tickets and wants to discover recurring issue types for routing. There are no labels yet. Clustering can suggest groups, but the group numbers are not facts until people inspect examples and connect them to action.

The first decision is the representation: raw counts, engineered features, or embeddings. The second is the distance meaning. If distance does not match the product question, the clusters will look scientific while being useless.

blocks.analogy: A cluster is a sticky note on a messy wall, not the wall itself.

spans.text: Question: can we find ticket themes that deserve new routing queues? Data: ticket-title embeddings plus metadata for language and product. Check: sample 20 tickets per cluster, name the theme, estimate purity, and test whether routing would reduce resolution time.

blocks.title: Cluster meaning
blocks.prompt: What should you treat a cluster label as at first?

options.text: A verified customer segment by definition.
A hypothesis to inspect and validate.
A supervised target label with no review needed.

blocks.explanation: Unsupervised outputs need interpretation and checks.

modules.title: k-means assumes compact round-ish groups
modules.sub: Centroids work best when distance to a center is meaningful.
modules.summary: k-means partitions data around centroids and needs k chosen carefully.
objectives: Choose k with evidence rather than default habit.

spans.text: k-means chooses k centroids, assigns each point to the nearest centroid, then moves centroids to the average of assigned points. It works best when clusters are roughly compact and similar in scale. It struggles with long curved shapes, very different densities, and strong outliers.

With k=4, sampled clusters look like billing failures, login issues, cancellation questions, and miscellaneous. The first three are useful; the fourth is a warning that k may be too small, representation may be weak, or the data contains many rare themes.

modules.title: DBSCAN finds dense regions and noise
modules.sub: Density clustering can reject outliers instead of forcing every point into a group.
modules.summary: DBSCAN groups dense neighborhoods and labels sparse points as noise.
objectives: Explain epsilon, min_samples, and noise in plain language.

blocks.title: Not every point deserves a cluster

spans.text: DBSCAN asks whether a point has enough neighbors within a radius. Dense regions become clusters; isolated points become noise. This is useful when you expect repeated issue pockets plus unusual one-off tickets. It is sensitive to scaling and radius choice.

options.name: k-means

cells.text: must choose k; outliers get forced into clusters

options.whenToUse: You expect roughly balanced compact groups.

options.name: DBSCAN

cells.text: clusters are dense neighborhoods separated by sparse regions
epsilon/min_samples sensitive; varying densities are hard

options.whenToUse: You expect noise and irregular cluster counts.

modules.title: PCA and UMAP make structure inspectable
modules.sub: Dimensionality reduction creates views, not proof.
modules.summary: PCA gives linear components; UMAP creates nonlinear low-dimensional embeddings.
objectives: Run a tiny PCA plus clustering example.

blocks.title: PCA plus k-means on a built-in dataset
blocks.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

X, _ = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
points_2d = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=7).fit_transform(X_scaled)
labels = KMeans(n_clusters=3, random_state=7, n_init='auto').fit_predict(X_scaled)

print(points_2d[:3].round(2).tolist())
print(labels[:10].tolist())

spans.text: This code projects data for inspection but clusters in the scaled original feature space. In real ticket work, inspect examples from each cluster before assigning meaning.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict why the code clusters X_scaled rather than points_2d.
predictThenReveal.answer: The 2D PCA view loses information. It is useful for inspection, but clustering the richer scaled features usually preserves more signal.

blocks.title: UMAP preserves local neighborhoods for exploratory maps

spans.text: PCA is linear: it finds directions of maximum variance. UMAP is nonlinear: it tries to preserve local neighborhood relationships when projecting high-dimensional data into two or three dimensions. That makes UMAP useful for visual exploration of embeddings, but the map depends on settings such as n_neighbors, min_dist, metric, and random seed.

Failure mode: a UMAP plot can create visually separated islands even when business meaning is weak. Treat island labels as hypotheses, inspect examples, rerun with different seeds/settings, and never use 2D distance as proof of category truth.

options.name: PCA
options.whenToUse: Fast baseline, compression, or linear structure.

cells.text: local neighborhood structure in a nonlinear map
settings and randomness can change visual clusters

spans.text: Checklist: features are scaled when distance matters; k or epsilon choice is justified; projection method and parameters are recorded; cluster samples are inspected; stability is checked across seeds or samples; and plots are not treated as proof of business categories.

modules.title: Cluster labels need validation and human meaning
modules.sub: The output becomes useful only when it changes a decision.
modules.summary: Unsupervised exploration ends with review, stability checks, and downstream tests.
objectives: Avoid using cluster IDs as target labels too quickly.
Plan the next supervised or routing experiment.

blocks.title: A cluster earns a name by surviving inspection

spans.text: Useful validation includes sample review, stability across random seeds, sensitivity to scaling, agreement with known metadata, and downstream utility. If a cluster called "billing" does not reduce routing time or improve labeling consistency, the name may be decorative.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Use clustering to generate hypotheses; use review and downstream metrics to accept them.
blocks.useWhen: Use it when labels are absent and you need exploration, routing candidates, anomaly pockets, or dataset understanding.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid using cluster IDs as ground truth without inspection, stability checks, and a decision they improve.

blocks.title: Cluster validation
blocks.prompt: What is the safest next step after discovering a visually distinct cluster?

options.text: Immediately use the cluster number as a legal category.
Inspect examples, test stability, and connect the cluster to a useful action.
Assume the 2D plot proves a real-world group.

blocks.explanation: Unsupervised results need human and downstream validation.

ai.label: AI
ai.laymanDefinition: Software systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence.
ai.technicalNote: In these foundations lessons, AI is the broad field; the concrete mechanisms are models, data, objectives, and evaluation loops.

ml.label: ML
ml.laymanDefinition: A branch of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of only following hand-written rules.
ml.technicalNote: ML work is defined by training data, features, models, objectives, validation, and deployment constraints.

model.label: Model
model.laymanDefinition: A learned or configured function that maps inputs to predictions, scores, clusters, or generated outputs.
model.technicalNote: Model choice encodes assumptions such as linearity, distance, tree splits, capacity, or sequential reward.

loss.label: Loss
loss.laymanDefinition: A numerical training signal that measures how wrong a prediction is for a task.
loss.technicalNote: Loss drives optimization; it is not the same as product quality, fairness, or final generalization.

generalization.label: Generalization
generalization.laymanDefinition: The ability of a model to perform well on examples it did not train on.
generalization.technicalNote: Generalization is checked with validation/test data, leakage audits, and slice monitoring.

pipeline.label: Pipeline
pipeline.laymanDefinition: A repeatable sequence of data transforms, feature steps, model fitting, and evaluation or inference.
pipeline.technicalNote: Pipelines prevent train/test leakage and keep preprocessing identical between training and production.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: Before you look anything up: in your own words, what is the difference between what k-means and DBSCAN use to decide whether two points belong together?
questions.acceptableAnswer: k-means groups points by minimizing distance to a centroid (center of a cluster), so it assumes round, similarly-sized groups. DBSCAN groups points by local density — a point belongs to a cluster if enough neighbors are within a set radius (epsilon); points in sparse areas become noise instead of being forced into a cluster.
questions.explanation: k-means assigns every point to its nearest centroid, while DBSCAN requires a minimum number of neighbors within epsilon — making density, not centroid distance, the deciding factor.

questions.prompt: Your dataset has customer segments that are elongated streaks and irregular blobs — definitely not round. Which outcome should you expect if you apply k-means?

options.text: k-means will correctly trace the elongated shapes because it minimizes within-cluster variance.
k-means will split or merge the irregular groups because it assumes compact, spherical clusters.
k-means will mark the elongated points as noise and ignore them.
k-means will automatically increase k to handle the irregular shapes.

questions.explanation: k-means pulls every point toward the nearest centroid, so non-spherical or elongated shapes get sliced along centroid boundaries rather than traced faithfully.

questions.prompt: A teammate runs DBSCAN on a dataset and reports that 40 % of points are labeled –1. What does that mean, and what should you investigate first?

options.text: 40 % of points formed a single large cluster labeled –1; the algorithm worked as expected.
40 % of points were classified as noise — epsilon or min_samples may be too strict for this data's density.
DBSCAN always reserves label –1 for the smallest cluster, so 40 % is the minority class.
The dataset has 40 % duplicate rows that DBSCAN automatically flagged.

questions.explanation: In DBSCAN, label –1 means noise — points with too few neighbors within epsilon. A very high noise rate usually signals that epsilon is too small or min_samples is too large for the actual density of the data.

questions.prompt: You use PCA to reduce 50 features to 2 dimensions and then plot the result. The clusters look perfectly separated. A colleague says 'Great — let's use the cluster IDs as our target labels and train a classifier.' What is the key risk they are overlooking?

options.text: PCA destroys all variance, so the clusters are meaningless after reduction.
Cluster IDs reflect geometric structure in the chosen features, not a validated real-world distinction — treating them as ground truth can encode noise or arbitrary splits into a supervised model.
A classifier cannot accept cluster IDs as input; they must be one-hot encoded first.
UMAP should always be used instead of PCA before clustering, making these results invalid.

questions.explanation: Cluster IDs are a hypothesis about structure, not confirmed labels — skipping human validation and jumping straight to supervised training risks teaching a model to reproduce an artifact of your feature choices or algorithm settings.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the practical difference between PCA and UMAP for exploring cluster structure?

options.text: PCA is only for images; UMAP works on any tabular data.

PCA finds linear combinations of features that preserve global variance; UMAP preserves local neighborhood relationships and can reveal non-linear structure, but its axes have no direct feature interpretation.
UMAP always produces better clusters than PCA because it uses more compute.
PCA and UMAP are interchangeable — the choice only affects runtime, not the shape of the output.

questions.explanation: PCA is a linear method whose components are interpretable combinations of original features; UMAP is non-linear and excels at revealing local groupings, but its 2-D axes cannot be mapped back to specific features the way PCA components can.
